```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%", dpi = 96)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

The Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) has been run nine times
since 1993. bdhs gives you all of it in one place: the official estimates
right away, and your own copy of the microdata in one line once you have DHS
access.

```{r setup}
library(bdhs)
```

## The surveys

```{r}
bdhs_rounds()
```

Functions take a `survey` argument, and you can refer to a round however you
like. Years, year ranges, DHS ids and DHS file codes all work:

```{r}
bdhs_survey_id(c(2022, "2017-18", 2018, "BD2014DHS", "4J", "1999-2000"))
```

`bdhs_surveys` adds fieldwork dates, sample sizes and implementing agencies,
and `bdhs_datasets` lists every one of the 441 data files the DHS Program
distributes for Bangladesh:

```{r}
bdhs_surveys[, c("survey_id", "survey_label", "fieldwork_start", "n_households", "n_women", "n_men")]
```

## Official estimates: no account needed

Every published DHS estimate for Bangladesh is bundled. `bdhs_official()`
returns tidy rows, and `bdhs_plot_trend()` draws them:

```{r}
bdhs_official("FP_CUSM_W_MOD")[, c("year_label", "indicator", "value")]
```

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
bdhs_plot_trend("FP_CUSM_W_MOD", by = "Wealth quintile")
```

See `vignette("maps-and-trends")` for subgroups, maps and more.

## Finding variables

`bdhs_search()` searches variable labels in the bundled codebooks, indicator
definitions and the harmonized variables together. `bdhs_variable()` shows one
variable across rounds and flags when its labels changed:

```{r}
bdhs_search("anemia|anaemia", where = "indicators")
bdhs_variable("v024", recode = "KR")
```

The codebooks contain names and labels only, never respondents' values.

## Microdata: the two-minute version

1. Register at <https://dhsprogram.com/data/new-user-registration.cfm> and
   request the Bangladesh surveys. It is free for research.
2. Download the files you need. The Stata format is recommended.
3. Point bdhs at them once:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bdhs_import("~/Downloads/BDHS")
```

From then on, any round and recode is one line away:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ir <- bdhs_read(2022, "IR")
kr <- bdhs_read(2017, "KR", vars = c("m14", "m15", "m17"))
```

`vignette("microdata")` explains importing, storage and the experimental
downloader.

## Practise with synthetic data

`bdhs_simulate()` generates fake data with the exact structure of a BDHS
recode: the same variable names, codes, labels and survey design. All the
examples in bdhs use it, and you can use it to write and test your code
before your DHS access comes through:

```{r}
kr <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "KR")
kr[1:5, c("caseid", "v001", "v022", "v024", "m15", "m17")]
```

Simulated values are random and must never be used for conclusions.

## A first analysis

Survey data need survey methods. `bdhs_design()` knows the clustering,
stratification and weights of every round:

```{r}
des <- bdhs_design(kr)
survey::svymean(~m17, des, na.rm = TRUE)
```

`bdhs_estimate()` goes a step further. It computes named DHS indicators with
correct standard errors, confidence intervals and denominators:

```{r}
bdhs_estimate(kr, c("facility_delivery", "csection"), by = "v025")
```
